common_name: Vermillion Sweet Potato (Early Red-Skinned Louisiana Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; Vermillion was bred at the LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station and matures noticeably faster than older Louisiana releases like Covington, so slips can go in slightly later and still finish before fall's first cool nights.

directions: Plant certified virus-indexed slips in well-drained, loose loamy to sandy soil after the danger of frost has passed and the ground has warmed; Vermillion is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release (formerly trial line LA13-81) bred to combine the deep orange flesh of established Gulf South varieties with a distinctive red-purple skin that stands out on the market table and holds its color well through months of storage. It was developed to mature roughly ten days faster than Covington, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a shorter window between transplanting and harvest and a bit more flexibility for late plantings or short-season sites. Roots size up reliably in both sandy and heavier garden soils, though as with any sweet potato, deep, loose ground produces the straightest, most uniform tubers. Cure freshly dug roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week before storing to heal skin wounds and convert starches to the sugars that give sweet potatoes their flavor.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions

common_name: Sakura Sweet Potato (Fast-Maturing Purple-Skinned Louisiana Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained, loose soil in full sun; Sakura finishes well ahead of most Louisiana sweet potato releases, so it tolerates a later transplant date and still matures before fall weather turns.

directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained, loose garden soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants to allow vines room to run; Sakura is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release named for its deep purple skin wrapped around an unusual light purple flesh, giving cooked roots a soft lavender color rather than the deep violet of typical purple sweet potatoes. Its standout trait for Gulf Coast growers is speed — Sakura roots reach harvestable size in roughly 90 days from transplanting, well ahead of the 110-120 days most varieties need, which lets gardeners get a crop in even from a late-set planting or squeeze in an earlier harvest before hurricane season disruptions. Like other LSU AgCenter releases bred for the region, it carries resistance to southern root-knot nematode, a persistent problem in sandy Gulf Coast garden soil. Cure harvested roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week to heal the skin and sweeten the flesh before storage.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions

common_name: Bellevue Sweet Potato (Copper-Skinned Disease-Resistant Louisiana Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, loamy soil in full sun; Bellevue's strong resistance to root-knot nematode and common soil-borne fungal diseases makes it a dependable choice for gardens with a history of sweet potato problems.

directions: Plant certified virus-indexed slips in well-drained, loose loamy soil in full sun after the last frost; Bellevue is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release (trial line LA06-52) prized for its smooth copper skin with few surface indentations, bright orange flesh, and moist, sweet texture that holds a consistent shape and quality from field to plate. It carries good resistance to southern root-knot nematode along with the major fungal diseases Fusarium wilt and Streptomyces soil rot, all common problems in warm, sandy Gulf Coast garden soil that can cripple less resistant varieties. Bellevue also stores exceptionally well after curing, keeping its eating quality for months longer than many other varieties, which suits Gulf South gardeners who dig a large fall crop and want it to last through winter. Cure freshly dug roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week before moving them to cool, dry storage.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions

common_name: Monaco Sweet Potato (Disease-Resistant Rose-Skinned NC State Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Monaco needs two to three weeks longer than Covington to finish, so set slips out promptly once the soil has warmed to give roots a full season to size up.

directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; Monaco is a North Carolina State University release valued for a broad disease-resistance package — it stands up to Fusarium wilt, Streptomyces soil rot, and southern root-knot nematode, though it remains susceptible to guava root-knot nematode, an emerging pest in parts of the South. Its rose-pink skin fades somewhat in storage over dark orange flesh, and the plant grows in a dense, upright habit rather than sprawling widely, which helps it shade out weeds within the row once established. Monaco needs a longer season than standard varieties like Covington — plan on two to three extra weeks in the ground — and while its disease resistance makes it a strong option for low-spray or organic plantings, expect somewhat lower yields than top commercial varieties. Cure roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week to heal the skin and develop full sweetness before storing.

common_name: Purple Majesty Sweet Potato (Deep Purple Flesh, High-Anthocyanin NC State Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Purple Majesty does not tolerate wet, poorly drained ground, so avoid low or flood-prone beds where Gulf Coast summer downpours can pool.

directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after the last frost; Purple Majesty is a North Carolina State University release with dark purple skin and equally dark purple flesh throughout, colored by a high concentration of anthocyanin pigments that give cooked roots a moderately dry texture and mild sweetness. It produces uniform, elliptic roots and performs especially well on sandy ground, reaching harvest in around 100 days from transplanting. The variety resists Fusarium wilt but remains susceptible to Streptomyces soil rot and both southern and guava root-knot nematodes, so rotate away from beds with a recent history of those problems. Purple Majesty ships and stores well after curing, but it does poorly in wet or flooded soil, so Gulf Coast gardeners should plant it on raised beds or well-drained ground rather than low-lying areas prone to standing water after heavy rain.
sources: North Carolina State University — NC Plant Breeding Consortium sweetpotato cultivar profiles

common_name: Purple Splendor Sweet Potato (Color-Fast Purple Flesh NC State Release)

planting.note: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun, and space plants generously; Purple Splendor is an unusually prolific plant producer and can overcrowd the row if set too closely. Avoid heavy, flood-prone ground, since it cannot tolerate standing water.

directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants a bit wider than usual since Purple Splendor produces slips prolifically and quickly crowds a tightly spaced row; Purple Splendor is a North Carolina State University release notable for purple flesh pigment that stays vivid through cooking rather than fading the way many purple sweet potato varieties do. Roots form uniform blocky to round-elliptic shapes and stay compact even in deep sandy soil, with a moderately dry texture and moderate sweetness once cured. It carries resistance to Fusarium wilt, Streptomyces soil rot, and southern root-knot nematode, though it remains susceptible to guava root-knot nematode. Purple Splendor stores and ships well but cannot tolerate flooded or poorly drained fields, so Gulf Coast gardeners should plant it on raised beds or well-drained soil rather than low spots that collect water after summer storms.
sources: North Carolina State University — Potato and Sweetpotato Breeding and Genetics Program variety descriptions
